newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn denies agreed EMU stability pact with Paris.
newsitem.headline: Bonn denies agreed EMU stability pact with Paris.

text.p: The German Finance Ministry denied press reports on Monday that Germany and France had agreed to set up a powerful new stability council to set economic policy for countries that adopt the euro single European currency.

The reports followed a row between France and the German Bundesbank, which sharply rejected a proposal from Paris for a political counterweight to the future European Central Bank (ECB), saying this would undermine ECB independence.
The German and French governments have rejected any plans to limit the independence of the ECB, that is due to start work with the launch of the single currency.

A Bonn finance ministry spokeswoman denied a report in the British Independent daily that said secret talks were underway to set up a stability council for countries that join economic and monetary union (EMU).

She said such a body would only be useful if it were informal and had no decision-making powers, citing remarks German Finance Minister Theo Waigel made at the Davos World Economic Forum in Switzerland at the weekend.
"There is no such agreement (between Germany and France)," the spokeswoman said in response to a request. "Waigel said that a stability council would be informal with no decision-making powers."
The spokeswoman cited Waigel's comments that the ECB would be the top decision-making body in a future euro-zone and the planned stability council would not be able to alter its policy.
Waigel told reporters at Davos he favoured a French proposal for an informal stability council to coordinate policy among member governments after the launch of a single European currency.
"A body like this makes sense for countries in the third stage of EMU," Waigel said. "But it will not be allowed to infringe on the work of the European Central Bank."
The third stage of EMU is the planned launched of the euro currency in 1999.
